guidance:
Use only Table 1 to define structure and values. Do not take data from narrative text or footnotes; use them only to understand layout.

1) Table title and scope
- Set `table_title` to the exact caption of Table 1.
- Work strictly within the visual boundaries of Table 1. Ignore other tables and figures.

2) Columns and headers
- Reconstruct the header area from left to right before creating any cells.
- Add every explicit data column header to `columns`. This includes each group, arm, timepoint, and any separate statistics columns (e.g., standardized difference, risk measure) that have their own header cell.
- For stacked or multi-level headers (a top label spanning several subheaders), treat only the lowest-level headers as data columns. Build each data column label by combining the higher-level and leaf text into a single unique string, such as "Top: Leaf".
- Do not turn a purely grouping header into its own data column.
- If the leftmost label column has a header, include that header string in `columns`, but never create data cells for it; its contents become `row_group` and `row_label`.
- Every `column_label` used in `cells` must appear exactly once in `columns`. Do not invent totals, combined columns, or alternate spellings.

3) Row structure: row_group vs. row_label
- Use the first column to distinguish structure from data.
  • Section/category headings: typically span multiple columns or appear in a distinct style and are followed by several related data rows.
  • Data rows: aligned with values in one or more data columns.
- Treat each section/category heading as a `row_group`. All subsequent data rows that clearly belong to that section use that heading (verbatim) as `row_group` and their own leftmost text as `row_label`.
- Rows not obviously under any section heading use `row_group` = null.
- If a section heading itself has values on the same line, represent that line with `row_group` equal to the heading text and `row_label` = null.
- Do not swap roles: `row_group` is always the broader section or category; `row_label` is the specific item within that section. Never place an item name in `row_group` or a section heading in `row_label` for the same data row.
- When the same section heading or item text recurs, reuse the exact string so grouping remains consistent.

4) Cells and values
- A cell corresponds to one non-empty intersection of a data row and a data column.
- For every visible numeric or textual entry in the body of Table 1, create exactly one cell object with fields: `row_group`, `row_label`, `column_label`, `value`.
- Copy `value` verbatim, preserving digits, punctuation, spaces, parentheses, ranges, units, percent signs, plus/minus signs, and textual markers (including N/A-like text or dashes when they are printed as values).
- A printed zero is a real value and must be included.
- Do not create cells for blank table entries and do not infer, calculate, or move values between columns or rows.

5) Avoid missing, extra, and duplicate cells
- Work systematically row by row.
  • For each data row, scan across all data columns and add a cell for every non-empty table entry.
  • Do not emit cells for pure header or section lines that show no data values.
- Do not add derived totals, combined values, or subgroup cells unless they are explicitly present in the header and body of Table 1.
- Keep values attached to the exact `row_group`, `row_label`, and `column_label` where they are printed; do not reorder or reassign values.
- Each combination of (`row_group`, `row_label`, `column_label`) must be unique. Never emit more than one cell for the same position.

6) String consistency
- Use table wording verbatim for `table_title`, `columns`, `row_group`, `row_label`, and `column_label`, including spelling, capitalization, spacing, and symbols.
- Ensure every `column_label` in `cells` matches exactly one entry in `columns`, and that identical headings used as `row_group` are written identically across all related rows.
